newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Third World group warns WTO to stick to mandate.
newsitem.headline: Third World group warns WTO to stick to mandate.

text.p: A Third World group on trade and economic cooperation warned the World Trade Organisation (WTO) on Tuesday to deal with trade rules only, saying it had no mandate to handle sticky labour and social issues.

The Group of 15 (G-15) said at the end of a three-day summit in Zimbabwe its 16 members would coordinate their policies on WTO matters and resist any attempts to widen the mandate of the global organisation.

Except on the WTO issue, the G-15's final communique reflected none of the generally hardline, anti-Western statements expressed by some speakers, notably Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe and Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, at the conference.

Political analysts and conference sources said Latin American states in the G-15 had toned down and ensured pointed accusations that the U.S. and the West were economic bullies were not carried in the communique.
Mugabe urged the WTO to stick to issues of trade rules. "We have agreed to resist any attempts to bring labour and other social issues under the umbrella of the WTO," he said.

"There seems to be such an attempt or temptation," he added at a news conference at the closing session. At the opening on Sunday, Mahathir said Western countries were trying to push labour issues onto the WTO agenda to undermine the cheap labour advantage developing countries had over them.

On Tuesday, Mugabe said Third World states were facing tremendous problems in implementing WTO pacts, and G-15 ministers would meet before, or at the WTO's first biennial ministerial conference in December in Singapore to coordinate their views.

The G-15 retains its original name although it now comprises 16 countries, namely Algeria, Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Jamaica, Malaysia, Mexico, Nigeria, Senegal, Peru, Venezuela, Yugoslavia and Zimbabwe.
It said it was working on the admission of Kenya.
Mahathir called for greater cooperation in the Third World, saying it had to become more self-reliant against rich nations which he accused of selfishness and dictatorial tendencies.
"We should not despair because the potentials exist for us to exert our rights and ensure a better future for ourselves," he said, calling for a boost in trade and investment.
